variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Advanced image captioning is the controlled generation of useful language from visual evidence. A vision encoder represents the image, a language decoder proposes a sequence of words, and an evidence-and-policy layer decides which claims may be released.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Define the caption contract before choosing a model”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Purpose and audience
pairs.detail: Name whether the output is alt text, search metadata, a structured catalog record, or an editable creative suggestion.
pairs.explanation: Name whether the output is alt text, search metadata, a structured catalog record, or an editable creative suggestion. Define the expected language, length, reading level, and required details.

pairs.label: Evidence boundary
pairs.detail: List the visual regions, verified OCR, product metadata, or trusted context that may support claims.
pairs.explanation: List the visual regions, verified OCR, product metadata, or trusted context that may support claims. Keep unverified model inferences outside that boundary.

pairs.label: Policy boundary
pairs.detail: Forbid unsupported identity, protected-attribute, emotion, diagnosis, intent, and other sensitive inferences.
pairs.explanation: Forbid unsupported identity, protected-attribute, emotion, diagnosis, intent, and other sensitive inferences. Define when a specialist or human reviewer is required.

pairs.label: Terminal outcomes
pairs.detail: Return a grounded caption, a conservative partial caption, a review state, or an explicit no-caption result.
pairs.explanation: Return a grounded caption, a conservative partial caption, a review state, or an explicit no-caption result. Never hide weak evidence behind fluent prose.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. The core invariant is every released claim must be supported by permitted evidence and useful for the declared captioning task.

variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Advanced image captioning is the controlled generation of useful language from visual evidence. A vision encoder represents the image, a language decoder proposes a sequence of words, and an evidence-and-policy layer decides which claims may be released.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Choose an architecture for the evidence you need”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Region-attention encoder-decoder
pairs.detail: A CNN or detector emits spatial features and an LSTM or transformer attends to them while decoding.
pairs.explanation: A CNN or detector emits spatial features and an LSTM or transformer attends to them while decoding. Region-to-word maps are inspectable, but limited visual features can miss small objects and relations.

pairs.label: Vision Transformer encoder-decoder
pairs.detail: A ViT represents the image as patch tokens and a transformer decoder reads them through cross-attention.
pairs.explanation: A ViT represents the image as patch tokens and a transformer decoder reads them through cross-attention. Training is parallel, while autoregressive serving still emits tokens sequentially.

pairs.label: Pretrained multimodal generator
pairs.detail: A vision-language model reuses large-scale image-text pretraining and instruction tuning.
pairs.explanation: A vision-language model reuses large-scale image-text pretraining and instruction tuning. Broader capability also brings inherited data bias, open-ended wording, and more behaviors to constrain.

variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Advanced image captioning is the controlled generation of useful language from visual evidence. A vision encoder represents the image, a language decoder proposes a sequence of words, and an evidence-and-policy layer decides which claims may be released.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Evaluate sentence quality, grounding, and usefulness separately”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Reference consensus
pairs.detail: Compares weighted n-grams with several human references to estimate consensus wording.
pairs.explanation: Compares weighted n-grams with several human references to estimate consensus wording. It is useful for corpus comparison, but a reference set cannot enumerate every valid caption or every unsupported claim.

pairs.label: Semantic propositions
pairs.detail: Parses candidate and reference captions into scene-graph tuples and compares objects, attributes, and relations.
pairs.explanation: Parses candidate and reference captions into scene-graph tuples and compares objects, attributes, and relations. Parser errors and incomplete references still limit the result.

pairs.label: Image-text compatibility
pairs.detail: Metrics such as CLIPScore compare the caption with the image representation.
pairs.explanation: Metrics such as CLIPScore compare the caption with the image representation. They add a distinct signal, but fine-grained negation, counting, relations, and metric bias still require targeted tests.

pairs.label: Claim failures
pairs.detail: CHAIR measures object mentions that are absent from ground-truth objects.
pairs.explanation: CHAIR measures object mentions that are absent from ground-truth objects. Production evaluation should extend beyond objects to attributes, actions, relations, OCR, and sensitive inference.

variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Reference consensus: Compares weighted n-grams with several human references to estimate consensus wording. Semantic propositions: Parses candidate and reference captions into scene-graph tuples and compares objects, attributes, and relations. Image-text compatibility: Metrics such as CLIPScore compare the caption with the image representation. Claim failures: CHAIR measures object mentions that are absent from ground-truth objects.

variants.prompt: What is the lesson's core production invariant?
options: Release the caption with the highest decoder confidence.
Release every caption that contains all requested keywords.
Support every released claim with permitted evidence and make it useful for the declared task.
Use the same caption for accessibility, search, and editorial workflows.

variants.prompt: Why can a lexical constraint make a caption less trustworthy?
options: It can force a required word even when the image does not support the corresponding claim.
It always changes beam search into greedy decoding.
It removes every visual token from the encoder.
It guarantees that the decoder returns an empty string.
variants.explanation: A lexical constraint controls emitted language, not visual truth. Grounding must still validate the claim associated with the required token or phrase.
